# title: HIS-201 Ch. 3 — 4 Main Ideas
# short: 4 Main Ideas
# order: 4

Why Powhatan tolerated the English
column2: Powhatan considered the colonists a nuisance but let them survive because English trade goods and weapons helped him strengthen his rule and fend off Piedmont tribes.

column1: How Spain colonized the Southwest and Florida
column2: Spain held its northern borderlands with scattered military garrisons, cattle ranches, and Franciscan missions, with Jesuits as occasional rivals.

column1: Why Spain's northern colonies stayed small
column2: New Mexico and Florida were poor and dangerous, so few Spaniards settled there, and the colonies survived mainly as missions and military buffers.

column1: The lesson of Acoma
column2: The Acoma massacre taught the Pueblos that resistance brought terror, but Spanish brutality also destroyed the cooperation New Mexico needed to prosper.

column1: Why Spain kept New Mexico
column2: The Franciscans persuaded the Crown to keep unprofitable New Mexico by arguing that abandoning baptized Indians would betray Catholic duty.

column1: The causes of the Pueblo Revolt
column2: Forced labor, disease, famine, Apache raids, and Spanish repression of Pueblo religion united the Pueblos to rise against Spanish rule.

column1: How mercantilism drove colonization
column2: Mercantilism encouraged European monarchs to sponsor colonies because colonies supplied raw materials, bought finished goods, and increased royal revenue and power.

column1: The significance of the Virginia Company
column2: The Virginia Company planted England's first permanent colony, and its land and political reforms laid the foundation for Virginia's growth before its failures led to royal rule.

column1: Why Jamestown nearly failed
column2: Jamestown nearly collapsed because gentlemen refused to work, settlers lacked farming skills, disease and brackish water spread, and colonists demanded food from Indians.

column1: How Virginia's reforms attracted settlers
column2: The headright system, an elected assembly, and relaxed martial law attracted migrants and investment, allowing Virginia's tobacco economy to expand.

column1: The significance of the headright system
column2: The headright system rewarded planters who imported laborers with more land, so it drove the flood of indentured servants and the growth of large tobacco plantations.

column1: The consequences of the tobacco boom
column2: Tobacco profits drove relentless seizure of Indian land and constant demand for labor, causing Indian wars and dependence on indentured servants before slavery prevailed.

column1: The cycle of Indian wars in the Chesapeake
column2: The Chesapeake Indians, organized in an effective confederacy, went to war whenever a new generation of men came of age, in 1622, 1644, and 1675.

column1: How Maryland differed from Virginia
column2: Maryland combined family proprietary rule, Catholic leadership, and toleration for all Christians, making it both a Catholic refuge and Virginia's tobacco rival.

column1: How England took greater control of its colonies
column2: England tightened control by making Virginia, South Carolina, and Georgia royal colonies, passing the Navigation Acts, and adopting Charles II's consistent colonial policy.

column1: The causes of Bacon's Rebellion
column2: Falling tobacco prices, landless freed servants, Indian conflict, and exclusion from power united frontier farmers and ambitious gentlemen against Berkeley's government.

column1: How the Navigation Acts affected the Chesapeake
column2: The Navigation Acts strengthened England's mercantilist empire but restricted Chesapeake trade and deepened planters' distress as tobacco prices fell.

column1: How slavery evolved in the early South
column2: In the early Chesapeake some blacks were free or indentured and had more rights, but harsh slave codes followed once larger numbers arrived directly from West Africa.

column1: How slavery united white society
column2: As slavery replaced servitude, fear of the growing black population drew whites of all classes and religions into a racist consensus led by a new gentry.

column1: How the slave trade transformed West Africa
column2: Slave trading enriched African rulers who built stronger states, while warfare, kidnapping, famine, and disease drew interior communities into bondage.

column1: The scale of Atlantic slavery
column2: The Atlantic slave trade carried far more Africans than Europeans to the Americas, making African workers central to every plantation economy.

column1: The characteristics of the Caribbean sugar economy
column2: Sugar turned the English Caribbean into deadly, black-majority slave societies of great wealth, and Britain valued the West Indies as its most valuable American possession.

column1: How Caribbean planters controlled enslaved people
column2: Caribbean blacks never had a period of rough frontier equality, because sugar planters enacted brutal slave laws early to control the slaves who soon dominated the islands.

column1: The economic origins of South Carolina
column2: Land scarcity on Barbados sent planters to found South Carolina, which grew rich exporting rice and later indigo with the skilled labor of a black majority.

column1: How African expertise built South Carolina's rice economy
column2: South Carolina's rice wealth depended on enslaved Africans' knowledge of rice growing, yet white fear of the black majority produced Caribbean-style slave codes.

column1: How Carolina's Indian slave trade reshaped the Southeast
column2: Carolina traders turned Indian slavery into a major business, devastating Florida's missions and neighboring peoples until the Yamasee War ended the trade.

column1: The result of the Yamasee War
column2: The 1715 Yamasee War, fought because the Yamasees feared Carolina would enslave them next, nearly destroyed South Carolina, shrank the Indian slave trade, and taught southeastern confederacies to play rival European empires against each other.

column1: The trustees' plan for Georgia
column2: Georgia's trustees banned slavery and liquor and limited landholding so the colony could be a buffer against Spanish Florida and a refuge of small farms.

column1: How North Carolina, South Carolina, and Georgia differed
column2: South Carolina grew rich on rice and slaves, North Carolina stayed a poor colony of small farms and naval stores, and Georgia began as a slave-free buffer and refuge.

column1: How North Carolina, South Carolina, and Georgia were alike
column2: All three colonies began under proprietors or trustees, ended as royal colonies, and ultimately depended on plantation agriculture and enslaved labor.

column1: How Europeans changed Native American societies in the South
column2: Europeans spread disease, forced Indians into missions, seized land for tobacco, and drew them into the slave trade, wrecking older ways of life across the South.

column1: The common pattern of southern colonies
column2: Southern colonies shared staple-crop economies, close ties to English merchants, inequality among whites, racial slavery, and Indian dispossession.

column1: The staple crops of the southern colonies
column2: The Chesapeake specialized in tobacco, South Carolina in rice and indigo, and the Caribbean in sugar, tying each region's wealth to coerced labor.

column1: Why Indian-settler relations differed across the southern colonies
column2: Disease and slavery had nearly erased Caribbean Indians before English settlement, Chesapeake peoples fought back through a strong confederacy, and South Carolina drew many Indians into trading pelts and captives.

column1: How Powhatan built his power
column2: Powhatan extended his confederacy by collecting tribute, making alliances, and marrying daughters of prominent men, though some coastal communities resisted and western peoples threatened.

column1: How the Powhatan and English divided labor differently
column2: Powhatan men hunted and fished while women farmed corn, beans, squash, and melon, but English men, not women, tended Virginia tobacco fields.

column1: Why the first Jamestown settlers starved
column2: The first Jamestown settlers starved because they would not grow food, had no women until 1608, and chose a swampy, mosquito-filled site.

column1: How Powhatan and English warfare differed
column2: Powhatan's people adopted the women and children of defeated Indian rivals, while English retaliation killed Indian women and children.

column1: How plantation monoculture spread African slavery
column2: Plantation monocultures of tobacco, sugar, and rice required intensive labor, so African slavery spread through an expanding international slave trade that drew in whites, Blacks, and Indians.

column1: Why Native peoples first cooperated with Oñate
column2: Native cooperation with Juan de Oñate initially reflected an attempt to avoid earlier Spanish violence and build a mutually useful relationship.

column1: Why Oñate's New Mexico was impoverished
column2: New Mexico stayed poor because Oñate's expeditions found no gold, silver, cities, or Pacific port, and most settlers turned to farming and herding.

column1: What distinguished the Franciscans
column2: Franciscans followed St. Francis of Assisi, rejected property, remained celibate, lived by alms, wore sandals, simple robes, and rope belts, and ministered to the poor.

column1: Why Florida mattered to Spain
column2: Florida mattered to Spain as a defense against Atlantic pirates and rival colonies that threatened Spanish treasure shipping.

column1: Spain's two-stage policy in Florida
column2: Spain first induced or threatened Native alliances, then placed Franciscan missions and resident soldiers among allied villages, barely preserving control of Florida.

column1: What Florida's Native leaders gained and owed Spain
column2: Florida's Native leaders received trade privileges and diplomatic presents in return for excluding other Europeans, supporting Spanish wars, and collecting taxes for Spain.

column1: How Spaniards obtained Indian captives in New Mexico
column2: Spaniards obtained Indian captives through war, purchase of women and children, and slave raids against Utes, Apaches, and Navajos.

column1: Why Pueblo elders urged a return to the old religion
column2: In the 1670s Pueblo elders argued that rejecting Christianity and returning to the old religion could reverse epidemics, drought, famine, and raids.

column1: The significance of the Pueblo Revolt
column2: The Pueblo Revolt was the most successful pan-Indian uprising in North American history and checked Spanish power in New Mexico.

column1: Why historians compare Pueblo Revolt testimonies
column2: The Pueblo Revolt testimonies of García, Nanboa, and Juan had different informants, circumstances, and biases, so historians compare them rather than trust any single interrogation.

column1: What the Pueblo Revolt targeted
column2: According to Pedro García, the Pueblo Revolt targeted custodians, priests, Spaniards, their servants, and Castilian speakers, and rosaries were to be removed and burned.

column1: How England and France shifted toward colonization
column2: By 1700 France and England had shifted from occasional ship predation and cod fishing to active colonization, challenging Spain.

column1: What the Virginia Company planned to send and produce
column2: The Virginia Company planned to send poor, unemployed people and skilled craftworkers to produce gold, silver, furs, pitch, tar, and lumber.

column1: Why Jamestown's site was deadly
column2: Jamestown's colonists chose an inland peninsula to avoid Spanish attack, but its marshes bred mosquitoes, and dysentery, typhoid, yellow fever, and salt poisoning killed settlers.

column1: Why English youths became indentured servants
column2: English landowners converted cropland to sheep pasture, pushing young people to London, Bristol, and Liverpool and then across the Atlantic as indentured servants.

column1: The results of English retaliation after 1622
column2: English retaliation after 1622 killed a generation of young Indian men, drove the Powhatans west, and seized hundreds of thousands of acres for tobacco.

column1: How Chesapeake life improved after the tobacco boom
column2: When the tobacco boom weakened in the 1630s and 1640s, Virginians grew more corn and cattle, health improved, and freed servants established modest farms.

column1: How the Calverts organized Maryland
column2: The Calverts granted manors to friends and smaller farms to ordinary immigrants and charged every settler annual quitrents.

column1: How the three Navigation Acts differed
column2: The 1660 act monopolized colonial shipping, the 1663 act routed European imports through England, and the 1673 act taxed coastal trade and empowered customs officials.

column1: Why Chesapeake society fell into crisis in the 1660s
column2: Tobacco overproduction lowered prices, wealthy planters monopolized coastal land, freed servants became tenants or moved west, and Navigation duties drove small planters into debt.

column1: How the Virginia assembly provoked unrest before 1676
column2: The Virginia assembly lengthened servant terms and reduced voting rights for landless men, triggering servant mutinies and small-planter tax protests.

column1: How Bacon's Rebellion unfolded
column2: Nathaniel Bacon, excluded from Berkeley's Indian-trade monopoly, attacked friendly and hostile Indians, while both Bacon and Berkeley offered freedom to servants and slaves who joined them.

column1: The causes of Coode's Rebellion
column2: Maryland's discontent stemmed from the Calverts' political monopoly, Protestant–Catholic conflict, and demands for cheaper representative government.

column1: How Chesapeake politics stabilized after 1690
column2: After 1690 Virginia's old leaders and newcomers shared offices, Maryland Protestants and Catholics shared power, and Black slavery helped prevent renewed white conflict.

column1: Why early planters preferred English servants
column2: Early Chesapeake planters preferred English servants because lifelong Black slaves cost more and high death rates made short-term servants cheaper.

column1: How early Black and white bound laborers lived
column2: Early Black and white bound laborers shared work, living conditions, socializing, sexual relationships, theft, escape attempts, and punishments.

column1: How Africans were enslaved in the West African interior
column2: By the late seventeenth century many captives were seized in raids specifically for sale or caught while fleeing war, famine, and disease.

column1: What Virginia's late-seventeenth-century slave laws did
column2: Virginia's slave laws made manumission harder, barred free Blacks from owning white servants, outlawed interracial marriage and sex, and denied slaves protection from bare-back whipping.

column1: How racial laws divided poor whites from slaves
column2: Racial laws encouraged white contempt for Blacks and made poor whites less likely to unite with enslaved people against planters.

column1: How Virginia improved white settlers' opportunities
column2: Virginia lowered taxes, helped freed servants become farmers, and extended the vote to most white men, while stable tobacco prices and lower mortality improved prospects.

column1: How the Chesapeake gentry built and displayed wealth
column2: The gentry profited from slave-worked estates and selling neighbors tobacco, goods, credit, services, and hired slaves, and displayed rank through courts, Anglican churches, and militias.

column1: How Barbados shaped early South Carolina
column2: Barbados immigrants dominated early South Carolina politics, Carolinians supplied West Indian food and cattle, and rice drew Caribbean slave ships to Charles Town.

column1: How European rivalry transformed the Caribbean
column2: The Dutch weakened Spanish Caribbean trade, English buccaneers raided Spanish towns and ships, and the French and English then colonized the islands.

column1: The value of Caribbean sugar to England
column2: Caribbean sugar earned England more than all mainland American colonial exports combined, as plantations and slavery spread across the English and French islands.

column1: Why Caribbean whites moved to the mainland
column2: Land exhaustion and crowding on the sugar islands pushed freed servants and planters' younger sons toward the mainland colonies.

column1: How sugar changed European diets
column2: Caribbean slave labor turned sugar from a medieval spice and medicine into a staple sweetening English working people's tea by the mid-eighteenth century.

column1: Where power in the sugar economy lay after 1700
column2: After 1700 power came more from producing, shipping, refining, and taxing sugar than from consuming it.

column1: Why North Carolina stayed poor
column2: North Carolina's poor harbors and unnavigable rivers limited markets, so the colony relied on general farming and naval stores.

column1: Why most Carolinians resisted the proprietors
column2: Most Carolinians, especially Barbados immigrants, rejected the Fundamental Constitutions' proprietary authority and provoked Indian slave wars for profit.

column1: What Carolina traded with Indians
column2: Carolina colonists traded textiles, metal goods, guns, and alcohol to Indians for hundreds of thousands of deerskins.

column1: Why Indians joined the Carolina slave trade
column2: Epidemics, wars over hunting and trading lands, and displacement gave Indians opportunities to enslave weakened neighbors for sale to Carolina traders.

column1: Why the Yamasees attacked Carolina
column2: In 1715 the Yamasees attacked Carolina traders, posts, and plantations because they feared Carolina would enslave them next, carrying captives to St. Augustine for sale.

column1: How South Carolina recovered after the Yamasee War
column2: Postwar South Carolina invested in African slaves and rice, whose profits made its planters the richest social group in mainland North America.

column1: How South Carolina's white population diversified
column2: After 1700 Swiss and German Lutherans, Scots-Irish Presbyterians, Welsh Baptists, and Spanish Jews made South Carolina's white population more diverse.

column1: What encouraged white unity in South Carolina
column2: Economic recovery and fear of Spanish Florida and its French and Indian allies encouraged white unity after South Carolina became a royal colony in 1729.

column1: How early South Carolina slavery differed from later slavery
column2: Frontier conditions and Black militia service in the Yamasee War created temporary interdependence, until Caribbean-modeled slave codes turned South Carolina into an armed camp.

column1: What Georgia's trustees hoped to produce
column2: Georgia's trustees sought to aid the worthy poor, create small farmers, and produce silk and wine for England.

column1: What happened after Georgia's trustees repealed their restrictions
column2: After the trustees repealed land, slavery, and liquor limits, royal Georgia developed a diverse society and a rice-and-Indian-trade economy like South Carolina's.

column1: What drew settlers to the southern colonies
column2: For more than a century after 1598, empire, utopia, and independence drew settlers to New Mexico, Florida, the Chesapeake, the Caribbean, the Carolinas, and Georgia.

column1: How the southern colonies compared
column2: South Carolina and the West Indies were more opulent and unstable than Virginia and Maryland, but all relied on staple crops, enslaved labor, slave codes, and white racism.

column1: Why the Spanish empire and English royal dreams faltered
column2: The Spanish empire faltered because Southwest riches were scarce and the Pueblo Revolt succeeded, while Parliament checked English royal dreams.

column1: How colonial dependence ran through southern society
column2: Poor planters depended on richer settlers for land and leadership, while wealthy planters depended on English and Scottish merchants for credit and markets.

column1: The paradox of southern colonization
column2: European dreams of freedom in the Southeast and Southwest depended on the least-free people, enslaved Africans and Indians.

column1: How the southern colonies remained unstable
column2: Spanish and English southern colonies remained unstable and conflict-ridden for most of their first century as Native peoples resisted war, disease, and enslavement.
